                                            PROJECT NO. 58000

RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                §                   BEFORE THE
WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                            §
                                                            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                          §
IN THE ERCOT REGION                                 §                     OF TEXAS

      STEERING COMMITTEE OF CITIES SERVED BY ONCOR’S COMMENTS
           ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO
                16 TAC §§ 25.192 AND 25.193 AND NEW § 25.252

       The Steering Committee of Cities Served by Oncor (OCSC) submits these Comments

(Comments) to the Public Utility of Commission of Texas (Commission or PUC) regarding the

proposed amendments to 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) §§ 25.192 and 25.193 and proposed new §

25.252. The Proposal for Publication (PFP) requested interested persons to file comments by

August 11, 2026. 1 Therefore, these Comments are timely filed.

                                       I.     INTRODUCTION

       OCSC is a group of over 170 municipalities and political subdivisions that, as local

governments, participate and have a unique interest in the energy market. In one capacity, OCSC’s

members are significant consumers of electricity for a breadth of public functions, which are

critical to the health and safety of the Texans who live within their boundaries. These functions

are provided through public funds and, as stewards of these funds, OCSC’s members rely on just

and reasonable energy prices. Additionally, OCSC participates in energy policy making to

safeguard the health and safety of its constituents. A reliable power grid ensures OCSC’s citizens

have access to critical functions such as police, fire, ambulance, and emergency coordination.

OCSC, therefore, has an interest in the transmission cost recovery concepts at issue in this project.




       1
           Staff Memo w/MS Word version of PFP approved by the Commission at 07.09 OM (Jul. 10, 2026) (PFP).


                                                        1
                                      II.     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

        As requested, OCSC has provided a one-page Executive Summary at the end of this

submission.

                                    III.     GENERAL COMMENTS

        OCSC appreciates the opportunity to provide these Comments on the Commission’s

proposed amendments to 16 TAC § 25.192, relating to Transmission Rates for Export from

ERCOT [Electric Reliability Council of Texas]; § 25.193, relating to Distribution Service Provider

(DSP) Transmission Cost Recovery Factors (TCRF); and new § 25.252, relating to Large Load

Customer Tariffs. This proposal is meant to implement Section 6 of Senate Bill (SB) 6, which

requires the Commission to evaluate whether the existing methodology used to charge wholesale

transmission costs to DSPs continues to appropriately assign costs for transmission investment. 2

It also specifically requires the PUC to evaluate whether the Commission’s retail ratemaking

practices ensure that transmission cost recovery appropriately charges the system costs that are

charged by each customer class. 3

        OCSC agrees with Commission Staff that the existing four coincident peak (4CP)

methodology no longer promotes equitable allocation of transmission costs. 4                      The 4CP

methodology was originally intended to allocate transmission costs to those who impact system-

wide peak demand the most. However, as has been widely acknowledged and discussed among

stakeholders and the Commission, some market participants possess operational flexibility which

allows them to reduce consumption during the 4CP windows, thereby avoiding, at least in part,


        2
            Tex. S.B. 6, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025).
        3
            Id.
        4
          Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, Project No. 58484, Steering Committee of Cities Served by
Oncor and Texas Coalition for Affordable Power’s Comments on Commission Staff’s Draft Report on Transmission
Cost Recovery at 2 (Apr. 13, 2026) (Project No. 58484 Comments).


                                                     2
 their allocated share of system-wide transmission costs. Specifically, the recent proliferation of

large loads across ERCOT is comprised of loads that possess more operational flexibility than the

residential and commercial customers represented by OCSC. Since these large loads can reduce

consumption during the 4CP windows without significantly disrupting their core business

functions, they are able to shift costs onto the less flexible residential and commercial customers.

Given this, OCSC urged the Commission in Project No. 58484 to adopt a rule which more fairly

allocates costs according to actual transmission usage patterns. 5

        OCSC is encouraged that the PFP at issue replaces the current transmission cost allocation

methodology with a 12CP methodology for assigning wholesale transmission costs to DSPs, as

this is in line with its recommendation in Project No. 58484. 6 A 12CP allocator best recognizes

the realities of the modern grid, given scarcity and operational stress on the transmission system

are no longer isolated to a small number of peak summer intervals. 7 Winter peak, in particular,

also presents system risks that must be factored into today’s transmission cost allocation

framework. As recognized in Commission Staff’s draft report, adding a larger number of CPs to

the allocation methodology best mitigates peak avoidance behavior which results in cost allocation

misalignment. 8 Along the same lines, OCSC supports the PFP’s replacement of the current 15-

minute CP duration with a 30-minute interval, as this may further prevent customers from avoiding

transmission charges during the CPs. 9

(Project No. 58484 Staff Memo and Draft Report).

            Project No. 58484 Comments at 7.

         As a general policy matter, OCSC underscores that large load customers should be

responsible for all costs of interconnection and system upgrades needed to provide them service.

SB 6 itself identified that consumers in the State should be insulated from the costs attributable to

large loads. Thus, OCSC urges that the Commission in this rulemaking ensure that large loads

pay for the private benefit of transmission expansion to serve them. OCSC’s comments below

reflect this position, as well as address other specific concerns with the PFP. 10

                                  IV.     SPECIFIC COMMENTS

        OCSC offers specific comments related to the PFP below:

A. Definition of “transmission interconnection costs.”

        Under proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(13), the term “transmission interconnection costs” is

defined as “[a]ll costs associated with the facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade

the interconnection of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level

customers, to the existing transmission network, including interconnection lines, substation

additions or modifications, and associated equipment necessary to establish or modify service.”11

OCSC is concerned that this definition is unclear as to what costs actually qualify as “transmission

interconnection costs” and which do not. The definition is broadly defined so that the exact costs

required to “physically interconnect or upgrade the interconnection of a transmission-level

customer” are open to interpretation. This lack of clarity may result in confusion as to which costs

should be considered “transmission interconnection costs” versus network costs.

        As explained above, large load customers should be responsible for all costs associated

with the interconnection needed to provide them service. Any costs that are not captured under



          10
              At this time, OCSC has no comments in response to the Commission’s questions. However, it reserves
the right to respond to those questions at a later date if appropriate.
        11
             PFP at 12.


                                                       4
 the definition of “transmission interconnection costs” risk flowing through to network costs. To

maintain the dividing line between transmission and network costs, OCSC recommends that the

definition of “transmission interconnection costs” in proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(b)(13) include

more specificity as to which costs should be allocated to transmission interconnection costs.

       Along the same lines, proposed new 16 TAC § 25.252(b)(5) defines “transmission

interconnection costs” using the same definition above. 12                     For the same reasons, OCSC

recommends that this definition include similar specificity as to which costs should be considered

“transmission interconnection costs.” OCSC adds that it is not entirely clear in either definition

whether costs related to new transmission construction or those tied to the new 765-kilovolt (kV)

system are deemed “transmission interconnection costs,” given costs under the definitions are

associated with the “existing transmission network.” Considering large load customers will almost

certainly require new transmission construction and will also impact the new 765-kV transmission

lines, the definitions should explicitly account for their associated costs.

B. Transition from 4CP to 12CP.

       While OCSC supports the transition from a 4CP to 12CP transmission cost recovery

framework, the PFP as drafted leaves many unanswered questions as to the actual transition.

Proposed 16 TAC § 25.192(l) outlines that transition from a 4CP to 12CP billing demand.13

Specifically, it requires each Transmission Service Provider (TSP) to update its tariff within 30

days of the rule’s adoption, and the updated tariff must “change any references to 4CP billing

demand or the associated months to allow for the transition to ‘superseding billing demand

approved by the commission’ or similar language and many not include any other changes.” 14 Not


       12
            Id. at 31.
       13
            Id. at 23-24 (noting that the PFP incorrectly labels this subsection as 16 TAC § 25.192(j)).
       14
            Id.


                                                          5
 every TSP may have 12CP billing demand data to update its tariff with 30 days’ notice. Moreover,

it is unclear when ERCOT would be able to provide updated 12CP billing determinants. OCSC

recommends that the Commission take input from stakeholders and ERCOT to ensure that the

transition from a 4CP to 12CP transmission cost allocation methodology examines all relevant

considerations.

C. Large load minimum billing demand.

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.193(d)(1) requires a retail electric provider serving a large load

customer to be charged for that customer based on a minimum billing demand. 15 Proposed 16

TAC § 25.252(e)(2) includes a similar minimum billing demand, requiring a large load customer

which does not energize at the time that billing commences to be billed based on its contracted

peak demand until such time as the large load customer energizes. 16 OCSC supports the concept

of a minimum billing demand charge for all large load customers. In enacting SB 6, the Legislature

sought assurance that large loads expanding throughout the State pay for the private benefit of

transmission expansions to serve them. The minimum billing demand charge will ensure to a

degree that large load customers pay their reasonable proportion of investment on the system.

D. Class allocation factor value updates.

        Even though Commission Staff previously filed a petition requesting that DSPs annually

update the class allocation factor values used to establish TCRF rates in contrast to the currently

prescribed biannual updates, 17 the PFP maintains the requirement that DSPs update their TCRF




        15
             Id. at 28.
        16
             Id. at 33.
        17
            Commission Staff’s Petition to Require Annual Updates to Class Allocation Factor Values Under 16 TAC
§ 25.193(c), Docket No. 58923, Commission Staff’s Petition to Require Annual Updates to the Class Allocation Factor
Values Under 16 TAC § 25.193(c) (Nov. 3, 2025).


                                                        6
 twice per year (specifically, on March 1 and September 1). 18 For the same reasons it previously

articulated in Project No. 58484, OCSC supports Commission Staff’s initial recommendation to

require annual updates to the class allocation factor values. 19 As highlighted by Commission Staff

just this March, the growth of each rate class coupled with the fact that the class allocation factors

used for the TCRF rates are generally updated on a four-year cycle (i.e., in the DSP’s

comprehensive rate case) results in significant inequitable cost-shifting between customer

classes. 20 Annual updates to the TCRF allocation factors will reduce this rate volatility and prevent

negative cost impacts from large load facilities and technologies being improperly passed onto all

ratepayers. 21

        Separately, proposed 16 TAC § 25.193(g) requires each investor-owned DSP to file an

annual report with the Commission on December 1, which details the amount of revenue collected

from each customer class during the preceding year beginning October 1 and ending September

30. 22 OCSC has significant questions concerning the actual implementation of the PFP’s proposed

class allocation factor update requirement. For instance, it is unclear how these updated class

allocation factors will alter rates, if at all. The interplay between this annual update and the

proposed biannual updates to the TCRF allocation factors is also ambiguous.

                                          V.       CONCLUSION

        OCSC appreciates the opportunity to provide these Comments to the Commission. OCSC

looks forward to future work sessions, discussions, and opportunities for stakeholder engagement

 regarding this rulemaking to update wholesale and retail transmission cost recovery in the ERCOT

region.
